# Interactivity at scale: where does aggregation run?

::: notes
Every zoom or pan needs a new aggregate. Three ways to afford that: redo it on demand,
precompute it, or hand it to a query engine. Same Big Data | Small Data split as on
the architecture slide; what changes is where and when the left side runs.
:::

## Re-aggregate on demand, on the server

::: {style="--diagram-h: 330px"}
```{=html}
{{< include assets/diagrams/arch-on-demand.svg >}}
```
:::

- What the census demo does: every zoom or pan re-runs datashader in Python
- One full pass over the data per interaction; only the image travels
- Any question you can code, always on current data

::: notes
- The live demo: Bokeh in the browser sends the new ranges; the Panel / HoloViews
  server re-aggregates all rows in the visible range at screen resolution; back comes an
  RGB image (datashade) or the aggregate itself, one value per pixel (rasterize).
- The data stays on the server, in memory after persist() or out of core with Dask.
- Latency = one aggregation pass: the wall-time readout on the live slides shows it
  (well under a second for 300 M rows on this laptop).
- Flexible and always current, but every user interaction costs a full pass: fine for
  one analyst, expensive for thousands of users.
:::

## Precompute: tiles and data cubes

::: {style="--diagram-h: 380px"}
```{=html}
{{< include assets/diagrams/arch-precompute.svg >}}
```
:::

- Compute once, serve many: each interaction is a lookup
- Fast, but limited to the choices made in advance

::: small
**Racial Dot Map** (Cooper Center, UVA, 2013; now offline): prerendered tiles, one dot per person · **Nanocubes** (Lins, Klosowski, Scheidegger 2013): in-memory spatiotemporal data cube · **imMens** (Liu, Jiang, Heer 2013): binned "data tiles", brushed on the GPU
:::

::: notes
- Ahead of time, a batch job aggregates everything at every zoom level: a tile pyramid
  (zoom level z has 2^z × 2^z tiles; the tile keys are the Z-order quadkeys from the
  framework section) or a data cube (aggregates for combinations of dimensions).
- At view time the browser only fetches what its viewport needs: a lookup, no pass over
  the rows, cheap to serve to many users (static files, a CDN).
- The price: only the precomputed choices. The HoloViz census notebook contrasts the
  Racial Dot Map with datashader: pre-rendered tiles "are fast to view but limited to
  the specific plotting choices they made". New data means a rebuild.
- Racial Dot Map: Dustin Cable, Weldon Cooper Center, University of Virginia, 2013;
  308,745,538 dots from the 2010 census; taken offline by the Center (statement
  archived Dec 2022).
- Nanocubes: IEEE TVCG 19(12), 2013: aggregation queries over billions of records at
  interactive rates, in memory. imMens: Computer Graphics Forum 32(3), 2013:
  multivariate binned data tiles, queried and rendered in parallel with WebGL at ~50
  fps. Both are research prototypes, no longer maintained.
:::

## Push aggregation into a query engine

::: {style="--diagram-h: 330px"}
```{=html}
{{< include assets/diagrams/arch-query-engine.svg >}}
```
:::

- Each view sends SQL; the engine aggregates; the browser gets a small result
- **Mosaic** (Heer & Moritz, 2023): views query DuckDB; linked views get pre-aggregated tables at pixel resolution
- **VegaFusion** (Kruchten, Mease, Moritz, 2022): Vega and Altair transforms run in a Rust query engine

::: notes
- The aggregation is expressed as a query: bin x and y, GROUP BY the bins, count or
  average. A modern columnar engine scans only the columns it needs, vectorised and in
  parallel.
- Mosaic: J. Heer, D. Moritz, IEEE TVCG 30(1), 2024 (VIS 2023); idl.uw.edu/mosaic. A
  coordinator collects the views' queries, runs them in DuckDB, and builds
  "materialized views" of data pre-aggregated at the level of input pixels, so linked
  selections stay fast: a small data cube built on demand. DuckDB runs on a server, in
  the browser (DuckDB-WASM) or in the Jupyter kernel (mosaic-widget).
- VegaFusion: N. Kruchten, J. Mease, D. Moritz, IEEE VIS 2022; vegafusion.io. Splits a
  Vega spec into a browser part and a server part; the server part runs on Apache
  DataFusion. In Altair: alt.data_transformers.enable("vegafusion"). Part of the Vega
  organisation since 2024; maintained, releases infrequent.
- "Query engine" rather than "database": DataFusion is an engine without a database.
:::

## Three architectures compared

|                    | Latency per interaction | Data freshness | Query flexibility | Cost / infrastructure |
|--------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|----------------|
| **Re-aggregate on demand** | one pass over the data | always current | anything you can code | a live server holding the data |
| **Precomputed tiles / cubes** | a lookup | stale until rebuilt | only what was precomputed | heavy preprocessing and storage, cheap serving |
| **Query engine** | one query; engine optimisations help | as current as the database | what SQL can express | an engine: server, kernel or browser |

::: notes
- Qualitative, not benchmarks.
- Real systems mix them: datashader over precomputed aggregates; Mosaic's
  pre-aggregated tables are a small data cube built on demand; map tiles are cached
  renders of on-demand queries.
- Rule of thumb: one analyst exploring freely → on demand; many users, fixed views →
  precompute; data already in a warehouse or lake → push the query down.
:::
